newsitem.title: ITALY: FOCUS-Italian jobless total climbs, no let-up in sight.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Italian jobless total climbs, no let-up in sight.

text.p: Italian unemployment, one of the biggest blots on the country's economic landscape, hit new highs in April as the labour market failed to absorb a growing workforce.
National statistics office Istat said on Wednesday that unemployment rose to 12.5 percent in April against 12.4 percent in January and 12.3 percent in the same month last year.

The actual number of people looking for a job grew 59,000 to 2.88 million -- the highest level since new unemployment statistics were introduced in 1992. The situation was especially acute in the south of the country.
"We should now make a further effort to do everything possible to revive the economy," Treasury Minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampihe told a banking conference after receiving the data.

But analysts saw little chance of a swift recovery for the sluggish economy and said they expected Italy's jobless total, already well above the European Union average of 10.9 percent, to increase in the months ahead.

"We probably won't see a structural fall in unemployment until at least the middle of next year when we hope to have a strengthening of the economic pick-up," said Pia Saraceno, director of the Italian Institute for Social Research (IRS).
Istat said the total number of employed rose 17,737 in April to 20.09 million, but this was not enough to absorb a 1.5 percent increase in the workforce.
Employment in the agriculture and industry sectors fell by 1.7 percent while the service sector saw a 1.1 percent rise.
"Overall we have a picture of stagnation. The number of people in work is basically the same but a larger number of people are now looking for a job," an Istat spokeswoman said.

The disparity between Italy's various regions remained marked, with a huge 22.5 percent of the workforce in the less developed south registered as unemployed against 10.7 percent in the centre and 6.7 percent in the wealthy north.
The differences among the young was even wider, with some 56.1 percent of youths in the south jobless in April compared with 18.8 percent in the north.
However, the situation was not thought to be quite as severe as the statistics suggest with many people believed to have unregistered, cash-in-hand jobs.

"The unofficial unemployment rate has to be lower than stated in some parts of the country, otherwise you would have a revolution on your hands," Saraceno said. "It's clear society has found some sort of stability," she added.

Prime Minister Romano Prodi's centre-left government has put the fight against unemployment at the top of political agenda alongside preparing state accounts for the launch of the single European currency.
Critics say the two goals are incompatible, with stringent budget cuts coupled to the Bank of Italy's tight monetary policy depressing the economy and thereby wounding job prospects.
Last weekend's summit of the Group of Seven (G7) leading industrialised nations heard a call on G7 members Italy, France and Germany to do more to deregulate their labour markets.

In a bid to boost access to work, Italy's parliament last week approved a package of measures aimed at loosening notoriously stringent labour laws, allowing firms more leeway to offer part-time positions and create job-share schemes.

Industrialists have said the measures do not go far enough, but trades unions, pointing to the low unemployment in the north, argue that more flexibility is not needed, just better infrastructure and job creation schemes for the south.
